note: Each entry names a guard and the mutation that removes it. guard-check applies the mutation and requires the named test to go RED. A surviving mutation means the guard has no proof, which is the condition the rc.6 audit found twice and this registry exists to make a machine judgement. expectedMatches is also the drift detector: if a guard gains or loses a site, the count stops matching and the entry fails before the mutation is applied.

guards.rationale: integerValue is the single arbiter of integer-ness for the knowledge pagination flags. Bare Number() sent NaN into core, which reported a typo as a range refusal.
Same arbiter on the sibling flag. Held separately because a fix that covered only one of the pair would otherwise pass.
A truthy guard cannot tell an empty flag value from an absent one, and swallowed --segment-events= entirely.
migration-plan --target-version abc answered WORKSPACE_MIGRATION_DOWNGRADE with the message NaN: a syntax error dressed as a judgement about versions.
Same class on the knowledge marker verbs, which reported the NaN as a promotion-version refusal without naming the flag.

includes(String(x)) admits a single-element array, a toString object, and a boxed String onto a legal enum member. This is the site that required an Owner exemption to Constraint 1. The mutation restores the exact pre-fix text from 6cf5c70 rather than simply deleting the typeof check: deleting it leaves governedAction as unknown and the pinned compiler rejects the file, which would prove the compiler bites and say nothing about whether the test does.
extension-registration appliesTo admitted [["work"],["work"]] through both the membership test and the duplicate test, because Set dedupe is identity-based.

Batching the privacy scan introduced an explicit maxBuffer, and an overflow there had to stay distinguishable from a command that simply failed. A blanket result.error check would reclassify ENOENT and ETIMEDOUT.

The mutation claim is released at every non-crash escape. The crash point keeps the claim on purpose, because a real SIGKILL never runs a finally and the retained claim is what marks the store mid-write.
guards.testName: WSC-2: knowledge-rebase enforces CAS and fails closed at fault points leaving the store locked

guards.rationale: The quarantine name must start with a prefix the residue gate recognises. stale-recovery- matched neither RESIDUE_PREFIX nor .gitignore, so a leaked quarantine file was invisible to the residue gate, entered the backup manifest, and could be committed and shipped to every cloner.
guards.testName: WSA-7b: a reclaimed recovery claim quarantines under a residue-visible prefix

guards.rationale: readSourceFile asserts nlink === 1, which is right for tracked source and a category error for a package manager's tree: pnpm hardlinks from a content-addressable store, so every CI runner failed SOURCE_HARDLINK while a cross-filesystem local store stayed green. The relaxation is scoped to a caller that names it; this entry pins that removing the scope reddens.

The hardlink relaxation is scoped to a package manager tree. As first written that scope was a comment, so a later caller could aim the reader at a tracked source file and drop the guard for that read with nothing to say so -- documented, not enforced, in the very function added to fix a misapplied guard.

The ppid===1 orphan-pattern branch catches a leaked load whose process-group leader already exited and whose pgid is a defunct group we never see registered live — the exact 2026-07-24 shape (35 yes orphans reparented to init). Without it, that class of orphan goes undetected.
guards.testName: BR: the orphan-pattern backstop catches orphans whose group was never registered

guards.rationale: The registered-group branch reports any process still alive in a group the session declared it owns, including non-orphan members whose leader is still running (a dev server left behind). Without it, only reparented orphans are caught and a still-parented leak escapes.
guards.testName: BR: a registered group with a live non-orphan member is residue

guards.rationale: A Release (sprint / release-train batch) is enforced parentless via the expectedParent map, so the timebox axis never entangles the scope tree. Without it a sprint could be parented under an Initiative, confusing membership (advisory:sprint) with parentage.
guards.testName: sprint: a Release is created parentless

guards.rationale: annotateWork validates a sprint reference is a well-formed {workspaceId, workId} qualified pair before storing it, so a malformed member tag cannot enter the chain. Without it a garbage sprint value would be accepted and later fail replay for every reader.
guards.testName: sprint: a valid sprint annotation is stored and round-trips

guards.rationale: The work.created reducer branch re-validates advisory value-shape so a forged/tail-appended create cannot smuggle a malformed advisory:* value past the envelope-only graph validator (the annotate path already validates; this closes the create door). Load-bearing for tamper-log integrity of every advisory key.
guards.testName: sprint: a forged work.created carrying a malformed advisory value fails replay closed

guards.rationale: The v2 activation receipt validator requires every entry realpath to be its declared path resolved under the admitted installation root. Without it the uninstaller -- which unlinks entry.realpath verbatim -- deletes whatever three readable files a self-authored receipt names, reachable from adapter-deactivate with no operator authority; the content/identity digests only prove the caller could READ the target. Found by adversarial review with an executed proof of concept.
guards.replace: entryRealpath === entryRealpath && expectedRealpath === expectedRealpath && admittedRoot.length >= 0 && sep.length >= 0
guards.testName: INC-001: an activation receipt may only name files inside its own installation root

guards.rationale: The Codex hook definition must shell-quote the handler path derived from the installer-admitted absolute project root. A relative command inherits the host fire-time cwd and can execute another project's same-named handler after the operator approved different bytes.
guards.testName: INC-002: Codex hook command executes the admitted root from an attacker cwd

guards.rationale: The Claude activation fragment carries the same admitted-root invariant. A relative handler path can be redirected by the host fire-time cwd even though the fragment digest itself was approved.
guards.testName: INC-002: Claude hook command executes the admitted root from an attacker cwd

guards.rationale: A host_observed_active receipt can only be constructed from a WeakSet-branded activation-host observation context or a pinned observation file. Removing the brand check would let a caller forge a plain object or structured clone into the authority-bearing output path.
guards.testName: ACT13: self-described, tampered, forged, cloned, and mismatched observations cannot mint activation

guards.rationale: The emitted SessionStart summary is a line-oriented document. Removing the control-character screen lets a tampered project.json forge extra context lines -- including a role assignment -- inside the 1024-byte budget, which no upstream validation can catch because the tampering happens after installation.
guards.testName: INC-014: a control character in a project field suppresses the whole summary instead of forging a context line

guards.rationale: The operator approves one command line naming session-start.mjs. Removing the fire-time self-digest check lets every later same-user write to that file run under the original approval, and makes the digest in the approved command line decorative.
guards.testName: INC-015: the handler refuses to run on bytes the approved command line did not pin

guards.rationale: mutates and authorityBearing are two different authorization categories and the operator bundle keeps their grant lists disjoint. A dispatcher that tested mutates first would satisfy an entry declaring both with a writeCommands grant alone -- a write grant carrying authority-bearing output, which operator-authority-v1 forbids. The MCP surface that did so is retired (STORY-287); the disjointness it depended on is asserted here so the rule outlives it. Nothing else refuses the flag pair: the schema declared authorityBearing with no dependency on mutates.
guards.testName: INC-016: no catalog entry is both a governed write and authority-bearing output

guards.rationale: An operator-pinned observation document has no self-limiting lifetime. Without the window comparison the same bytes, re-pinned under a rotated bundle generation, mint another host_observed_active receipt indefinitely. This comparison is the only thing tying a recorded fire to the authority that was current when it happened.
guards.testName: INC-017: a pinned observation cannot be replayed past the window that admitted it

guards.rationale: The window bound alone admits an observedAt that is inside the bundle window but still in the future relative to the clock that reads it. A far-future observedAt would then survive every future window. Nothing can be observed after the moment of verification.
guards.testName: INC-017: a pinned observation cannot be replayed past the window that admitted it

guards.rationale: The catalog's authorityBearing flag was enumerated by a test, not enforced against what a verb emits, so a future command minting activationState/hookFired/trustApprovalObserved without the flag reddened nothing and shipped over MCP as a read-only tool. The CLI write boundary now refuses undeclared host-state output for every verb, present or future. Removing it restores a surface where caller-supplied input can be dressed as host evidence.
guards.testName: INC-012: authority-shaped output from a verb that does not declare it fails closed

guards.rationale: The activation merge admits only canonical settings bytes. A non-canonical absent-file stand-in fails ACTIVATION_FRAGMENT_INVALID for every root that has no .claude/settings.json yet -- the ordinary first install -- before anything is written.
guards.testName: INC-022: activation installs into a root that has no .claude/settings.json yet

guards.rationale: event-list is the only list verb whose records are verbatim, so it is the only one whose page can outgrow the canonical ceiling. The catch turns the protocol's INPUT_OVERSIZED into a page-specific refusal that names the flag to lower. Removing it restores export's own code on a paged read -- a caller told 'this chain cannot be read this way' by the verb that exists to read it, which is INC-004's absence-instead-of-refusal defect one layer down.
guards.testName: INC-027: a page that cannot fit is refused under its own code, never shortened

guards.rationale: readMetadata's `admit` default is the only thing standing between a relocation-aware engine and a relocation-blind one. Flipping it to a permissive value breaks nothing visible: every caller keeps working, every existing test stays green, and the entire mechanism is silently off because six call sites -- including acquireWorkspaceLease, which is what makes coverage universal -- pass no admission argument at all. Restoring the guard restores a vacated address that still answers reads and still takes write leases.
guards.find: async function readMetadata(workspaceRoot: string, admit: WorkspaceAdmission = "live"): Promise<WorkspaceMetadata> {
guards.replace: async function readMetadata(workspaceRoot: string, admit: WorkspaceAdmission = "adoption"): Promise<WorkspaceMetadata> {
guards.testName: WSR-1 T4: the readMetadata admission default is strict

guards.rationale: walkControlTree collects FILES only, so the snapshot manifest is structurally blind to a copy that dropped an empty events/, views/ or backups/ -- such a copy verifies SNAPSHOT_VERIFIED and then fails at the first read after it has already been bound. Removing this assertion does not merely weaken adopt; it moves the failure from a named refusal before the commit point to an unexplained WORKSPACE_PATH_INVALID after it.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T8: the empty-directory gap is closed by the ADDED check, not by the manifest

guards.rationale: Without the workspaceId term the relocation roster still looks rigorous -- it still names an actor, still names destinations, still carries a basis -- and it permits every workspace on the machine. That is the permanently-green-gate shape this repository was burned by three times in one day: a check whose two sides cannot differ. Removing this term restores an authority for workspace X that authorizes moving workspace Y.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T14c: a roster scoped to a different workspaceId does not permit this workspace

guards.rationale: The destinations term was ruled in D6 and pinned by nothing: deleting it left the whole suite green, so a permit authorising 'move workspace X to /approved/place' silently authorised '/attacker/place' too. The relocationId term does NOT subsume it -- the two are independently authored fields of the same document, so a permit can name the right hop and the wrong destination, which is a reachable operator error as well as an attack.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T14e: a permit scoped to a different destination does not admit this hop

guards.rationale: This is the term that makes the permit per-INVOCATION. Relocation never advances the event chain, so the {version, headEventHash} basis is byte-identical after a hop and bounds drift rather than reuse -- measured, not supposed: one authority file drove vacate/adopt/abort twice and left three live authorities for one workspaceId. Removing the relocationId term restores an authority document that can be spent forever.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T14f: a permit for a different hop does not admit this one

guards.rationale: Without the stage term one permit authorises every verb of its hop, which specifically means the abort can ride the authority its own vacate was minted with -- the exact move an adversarial review used to fork a workspace with engine verbs only and no tampering.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T14g: a permit for another stage of the same hop does not admit this verb

guards.rationale: Abort is the one verb that can create a fork, and the source cannot know whether the destination adopted. The acknowledgement proves nothing and is not meant to: it is the ceremony that stops the fork-creating verb from being one flagless command away. Removing it removes the only in-band statement that the operator was told.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T27: abort demands its own stage permit, an explicit acknowledgement, and refuses on an adopted target

guards.rationale: The one mechanical check standing in front of the fork: when the operator can reach the destination and passes its own relocation-inspect document, an adopted destination refuses the abort outright. Neutering this turns a checked artifact into a decorative one -- the shape this repository has been burned by four times.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T27: abort demands its own stage permit, an explicit acknowledgement, and refuses on an adopted target

guards.rationale: abort called matchPermit and never assertPermitBasis, so the one verb that can create a fork was the only one whose authority was not basis-checked. It was harmless because a vacated chain cannot advance -- an invariant that lived in a different function and was written down nowhere.
guards.find:
assertPermitBasis(permit, trailing.basis.version, trailing.basis.headEventHash);
  // The vacate commitment.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T27: abort demands its own stage permit, an explicit acknowledgement, and refuses on an adopted target

guards.rationale: The third review measured the stage term as insufficient on its own: one authority document may legitimately carry vacate, adopt and abort permits for one hop, so a document minted BEFORE the vacate forked the workspace with one extra flag. The abort permit therefore names the sha256 of the committed vacated ledger entry -- which contains the sha256 of the file that authorised the vacate, so that document would have to contain a digest of itself. Removing this comparison restores the one-file, one-approval fork and erases the permanent two-different-authority-digests record in the ledger.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T42: an abort permit names the vacate commitment, so it cannot be the document that authorized the vacate

guards.rationale: Before the document carried a declared observedAt, an inspection taken before the destination adopted was BYTE-IDENTICAL to a fresh one, so the stale path needed no intent and stamped an affirmative verification into the receipt. Removing the window comparison restores exactly that: any document of the right shape, of any age, passes. The check bounds two caller-declared instants against each other and is NOT a freshness proof -- that limit is stated in the module header and in ADR 0003 rather than implied away here.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T43: a target inspection carries a declared observation instant and abort bounds it

guards.rationale: The admission conjunct that keeps `abort` admissible ONLY at a vacated address. Widened, relocation-abort executes at the DESTINATION and writes an aborted entry into the copy's own ledger -- the fork-creating move performed at the wrong end. Its partner check inside abortWorkspaceRelocation is a labelled restatement, not a second guard: with the admission intact no address can reach it, which is why this layer is the one registered.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T33: abort runs at the source address and nowhere else

guards.rationale: The mirror conjunct for adopt. Widened, an adopt aimed at the vacated SOURCE stops being refused by the state machine and falls through to adopt's own destination checks, which report a different problem than the one that exists.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T32: adopt restates the relocationId of the hop it is completing

guards.rationale: The verdict that refuses a third copy of an adopted tree. Changing the fallback to `live` makes every restored backup and every rsync-to-staging copy read as a fully live workspace on the readMetadata-only paths (lease acquisition, lease-break, lease-recovery-break) that the admission check exists to cover.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T34: a copy of an ADOPTED tree at a third address is a foreign address everywhere

guards.rationale: relocationStateAt returned `live` for ANY address whenever the ledger was absent, never comparing the address it was handed against the binding in the file. Since that state is the verdict word of the mandatory two-sided close-out, a stale pre-vacate copy or a restored backup read as a second live authority while every other verb refused to open it.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T30: a stale copy is not `live` just because it carries no ledger

guards.rationale: The cheapest detector of naive or accidental ledger corruption: an entry must name itself from its own content. Both pre-existing tamper tests deliberately recompute the relocationId in order to reach the chaining rule, which left this check with no red proof anywhere.
guards.find: if (entry.relocationId !== deriveRelocationId({ workspaceId, sequence: entry.sequence, from, to, basis })) {
guards.replace: if (entry.relocationId !== deriveRelocationId({ workspaceId, sequence: entry.sequence, from, to, basis }) && entry.sequence === 9999) {
guards.testName: WSR-1 T35: a ledger entry must name itself, and a completion must restate its hop

guards.rationale: A completion entry must restate its hop's id, from, to and basis. Without it an adopted entry can claim a binding its vacate never declared, which is how a ledger stops being the thing that makes a fork legible.
guards.find:
if (entry.relocationId !== previous.relocationId ||
        canonicalJson(from) !== canonicalJson(previous.from) ||
        canonicalJson(to) !== canonicalJson(previous.to) ||
        canonicalJson(basis) !== canonicalJson(previous.basis)) {
guards.testName: WSR-1 T35: a ledger entry must name itself, and a completion must restate its hop

guards.rationale: The single line that makes the verifySnapshotManifest call on the next line non-circular. Without it adopt compares the transported tree against a manifest the presenter of that tree also produced -- the manifest is unsigned canonical JSON, so forging one is free. A working exploit exists: tamper a view, regenerate the manifest, adopt clean.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T36: adopt binds the supplied manifest to the one the vacate recorded

guards.rationale: The resolved roots must BE the destination the vacate declared. Removing it lets an adopter declare arbitrary framework/transient/evidence-locator/release-trust roots, so the ledger commits a destination binding the host does not actually have.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T31: adopt binds the destination it was declared for, at the address it was declared for

guards.rationale: Adopt's proof of attention. The only wrong-id adopt in the suite ran against a tree with no ledger and stopped one line earlier at NOT_PENDING, so this branch was never reached by any test.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T32: adopt restates the relocationId of the hop it is completing

guards.rationale: A hop that leaves the workspace root in place commits, kills the source and can never be adopted, because relocationStateAt keys on that root and evaluates its vacated branch before its adoption-required branch. The shipped code accepted it; the only exit was abort, which is the fork-creating verb.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T29: a hop that does not move the workspace root is refused while the source is still alive

guards.rationale: The shape half at the input boundary. Without it a destination whose five roots collide or nest is refused only at the very end by the LEDGER validator, which reports relocations[4].to for a command line the operator typed as flags -- a ledger-integrity code for an operator input error, after a lease has been taken and a full control-tree manifest computed.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T29: a hop that does not move the workspace root is refused while the source is still alive

guards.rationale: vacate's explicit --expected-version compare-and-set. On the `head` route the two sides are computed from one read milliseconds apart and cannot differ; the explicit-integer route is the only one on which this check can be the one that fires, and it had no test.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T39: vacate's explicit --expected-version is a real compare-and-set

guards.rationale: The sixteen-entry cap, refused while the source is still alive. A vacate admitted into a ledger with no room for its own completion would brick the chain permanently: source VACATED, destination ADOPTION_REQUIRED, both completions LEDGER_FULL. It now lives in the preparation relocation-plan and relocation-vacate share, because while it sat at the commit point no read-only verb reached it: the plan answered PLANNED at a full ledger and sent the operator into the out-of-band minting ceremony for a hop the vacate would refuse. T40 asserts BOTH sides of that -- the plan refusing, and the vacate refusing with the source still alive.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T40: the ledger cap refuses a vacate while the source is still alive

guards.rationale: relocation-plan and relocation-vacate must derive the SAME relocationId, because the operator mints an authority against the plan's id and the vacate is what spends it. Perturbing the shared derivation makes the plan a prediction of a hop the engine is not about to take, and every relocation stops being authorizable at all.
guards.find: relocationId: deriveRelocationId({ workspaceId: state.metadata.workspaceId, sequence, from, to, basis }),
guards.replace: relocationId: deriveRelocationId({ workspaceId: state.metadata.workspaceId, sequence: sequence + 1, from, to, basis }),
guards.testName: WSR-1 T28: relocation-plan is the vacate's own preparation, and it writes nothing

guards.rationale: assertDistinctRootShape compares the five roots of ONE binding against each other and never `from` against `to`, so nothing forbade a destination nested inside the source workspace root. Such a hop relocates cleanly and leaves the only live control tree inside the directory the runbook's next step tells the operator to delete -- `rm -rf` on the vacated source then destroys the chain.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T29: a hop that does not move the workspace root is refused while the source is still alive

guards.rationale: A destination stated in a spelling the destination host does not realpath to refuses under FOREIGN_ADDRESS, which names the wrong problem -- the ledger DOES name that tree, under a different spelling, and recovery is abort-only after the source is already dead. The engine cannot discriminate it without probing a path on another host, so the inspection reports the near miss. Removing the report returns the operator to guessing.
guards.testName: WSR-1 T41: a destination stated in the wrong spelling is reported as a near miss, not just a foreign address

guards.rationale: A read taken with identityDrift:"collect" must never be branded as an installation. Branding it would hand uninstall, rollback and activation the very installation the strict reader refuses, turning the rebind path's read option into a force flag by the back door.
guards.testName: INC-219 a drift-tolerating read is NOT branded, so nothing downstream can act on it

guards.rationale: Rebind relaxes identity and nothing else. Without the content comparison it would re-bind a receipt to files whose bytes had changed, which is precisely the substitution the installation receipt exists to detect.
guards.testName: INC-219 rebind REFUSES when a byte changed, because content is the guarantee

guards.rationale: The extension index must summarise its collections, never carry them. Carrying them made the file grow with every line of governed prose written into the chain, and at 532 records it crossed the one-MiB canonical ceiling and took eight read verbs down with it (INC-198). Returning the records instead of their digest restores exactly that growth, so a test that does not notice is not proving the bound.
guards.testName: STORY-299: extension view size is independent of the prose inside the records

guards.rationale: The bound is only allowed because detection power is kept: each record is hashed whole, then the vector of hashes is hashed. Narrowing the per-record hash to the identifier keeps the file the same size and the same shape while making every edit inside every record invisible -- the cheapest way to turn a summary into a lie, and the one a size-only assertion would never catch.
guards.replace: records.map((record) => canonicalSha256((record as { readonly id?: string }).id ?? ""))
guards.testName: STORY-299: any single byte inside any extension record still moves the view

guards.rationale: The projection is evaluated before any segment is written so that a view which cannot fit is refused with the chain untouched. Moving it after the writes restores the ordering that produced INC-198 event seq 3842: the event lands, the projection then fails, and the caller is told its write was rejected while the fact is durable. STORY-300 generalised this path to a fold, so the two are no longer adjacent statements and the mutation reorders the whole span; that the anchor had to move is itself the record of a real restructure rather than a drifting comment.
guards.testName: STORY-299: an over-budget projection is refused with the chain untouched
